sentences.text: Brief facts of the case are that on 01.07.2017 at about 04:30 p.m., petitioner/injured Razzaque alongwith his sister-in- law and his minor son were travelling from Bulandshar to Mirzapur on motorcycle bearing no.DL-3SCS-5600.

When they reached near Mirzapur, U.P., a Maruti car bearing no.HR-51AB-8784(hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) came driven in rash and negligent manner from the opposite direction and hit the motorcycle from front right side.
Due to the impact, all three riders on the bike fell and sustained injuries.
Petitioner suffered a fracture in his right leg.
He was taken to JPN Apex Trauma Center, AIIMs, New Delhi where he remained admitted till 09.07.2017.

sentences.text: Certified copy of the FIR describes the manner of the accident and specifies the registration number of the offending vehicle.
The certified copy of the site plan further shows that both the vehicles were plying on the same road but in opposite directions.
Such site plan does not however specify the permitted direction of the traffic.

The site plan further clearly shows that while the motorcycle of the petitioner was on the extreme left side of the road, the offending vehicle which was initially plying on the extreme right of the road in the opposite directions, suddenly changed its lane in a diagonal manner and thereby caused a head- on collision with the motorcycle of the petitioner.
The site plan strongly suggests negligence on the part of the offending vehicle.

As regards delay of 12 days in lodging of the FIR, same has been duly explained by the petitioner by stating that since he was undergoing treatment in respect of the injuries sustained by him and his minor son, he could not immediately report the matter to the police.
Respondent no.1 and 2 also did not refute the occurrence of the accident or involvement of the offending vehicle or rash and negligent driving by Respondent no.1.
Medical documents also show that the petitioner remained hospitalized for about 9 days.
In these circumstances, a delay of 12 days in lodging of the FIR does not create a doubt as to genuineness of the claim.

As regards defence raised by the insurance company qua contributory negligence on the part of the petitioner in triple riding and not wearing helmet, it is seen that though the petitioner and the other two riders on the motorcycle may have violated the traffic laws by triple riding, the circumstances and CHARU Digitally signed by CHARU GUPTA Date: 2025.08.26 MACT NO.991/17 Razzaque v.
Arif GUPTA 17:06:41 +0530 P.No. 6 Of 23 BK the manner in which the accident occurs does not establish any nexus of the violation with the accident.
The accident is proved to have occurred due to sole negligence of respondent no.1 and triple ridding did not, in any way, contribute to the accident.

Merely, because it is the case of triple riding by the petitioner, there is nothing on record to show that such triple riding contributed to the occurrence of the accident particularly when it has been asserted by the petitioner and corroborated by the site plan that the offending vehicle/car came from the opposite directions and transcended into the lane in which the petitioner was riding his motorcycle.

Further, even if it is assumed that the petitioner and other riders were not wearing a helmet or a protective gear, the fact that the injuries have been sustained in the leg and not in the head, does not render them liable to contributory negligence.

sentences.text: The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have Digitally earned.

Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).

16.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof.

Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant.
Decisions of Hon'ble Supreme Court and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary.
16.6. Observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajkumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. is quoted hereunder:
"10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his Digitally signed CHARU GUPTA by CHARU GUPTA Date: 2025.08.26 17:07:11 +0530 MACT NO.991/17 Razzaque v. if the left hand of a claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or functional disablement may be assessed around 60%.
If the claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry.

sentences.text: In fact, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of `loss of future earnings', if the claimant continues in government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities as a consequence of losing his hand.

Sometimes the injured claimant may be continued in service, but may not found suitable for discharging the duties attached to the post or job which he was earlier holding, on account of his disability, and may therefore be shifted to some other suitable but lesser post with lesser emoluments, in which case there should be a limited award under the head of loss of future earning capacity, taking note of the reduced earning capacity.

It may be noted that when compensation is awarded by treating the loss of future earning capacity as 100% (or even anything more than 50%), the need to award compensation separately under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life may disappear and as a result, only a token or nominal amount may have to be awarded under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life, as otherwise there may be a duplication in the award of compensation.

Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law,
proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable.
Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of Razzaque Ahmed vs Arif on 26 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69748430/
3
In these circumstances, a delay of 12 days in lodging of the FIR does not create a doubt as to genuineness of the claim.
The accident is proved to have occurred due to sole negligence of respondent no.1 and triple ridding did not, in any way, contribute to the accident.
Merely, because it is the case of triple riding by the petitioner, there is nothing on record to show that such triple riding contributed to the occurrence of the accident particularly when it has been asserted by the petitioner and corroborated by the site plan that the offending vehicle/car came from the opposite directions and transcended into the lane in which the petitioner was riding his motorcycle.
Further, even if it is assumed that the petitioner and other riders were not wearing a helmet or a protective gear, the fact that the injuries have been sustained in the leg and not in the head, does not render them liable to contributory negligence.

The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have Digitally earned.
It may be noted that when compensation is awarded by treating the loss of future earning capacity as 100% (or even anything more than 50%), the need to award compensation separately under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life may disappear and as a result, only a token or nominal amount may have to be awarded under the head of loss of amenities or loss of expectation of life, as otherwise there may be a duplication in the award of compensation.
